title: Power needed for flight grows as length^3.5 while muscle power grows as length^3

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Power needed for flight grows as length^3.5 while muscle power grows as length^3

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A bird of fixed proportions must fly at a minimum speed proportional to the square root of its linear size, so the work needed for flight varies as the 3½ power of linear size while the work its muscles can supply varies only as the cube; flight thus becomes harder as birds get larger (about 1.4 times harder per doubling of length).

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: V_{min} \propto L^{1/2}; W_{flight} = mV^2 \propto L^{7/2}; W_{muscle} \propto L^3; per doubling of L: 2^{7/2} : 2^3 \approx 1.4 : 1

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The work requiring to be done, then, varies as the power 3½ of the bird’s linear dimensions, while the work of which the bird is capable depends on the mass of its muscles, and therefore varies as the cube of its linear dimensions.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Flight and size”. Scope: flying birds of similar proportions

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: V_{min} \propto L^{1/2}; W_{flight} = mV^2 \propto L^{7/2}; W_{muscle} \propto L^3; per doubling of L: 2^{7/2} : 2^3 \approx 1.4 : 1

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-06: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The scaling exponents give clear tests and open morphology plus movement data cover many birds. The exact energetic quantities require model-derived estimates and harmonization, so the claim is currently resolvable only under subsets and assumptions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across geometrically similar birds, fit minimum sustained flight speed and flight power against linear size and test exponents of 0.5 and 3.5, while comparing available muscle power with an exponent of 3. Deviations outside uncertainty or successful flight above the predicted power margin would refute the model.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Bird proportions and flight styles are not fixed across size.

Flight power and muscle power are seldom directly measured in open comparative datasets.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.6
data existence: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The exponents are explicit, and global wing morphology is public, so the geometric piece of the argument can be evaluated quickly. The work comparison itself needs flight metabolism and muscle fraction, which are scattered through wind-tunnel studies rather than present in that morphology table. Rival aerodynamic models also change the exponent, so existing open data test a restricted, model-dependent version of the claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From mass and wing area, compute the mechanical power required for level flight under the fixed-proportion argument and compare its scaling with size to available muscle power. The claim is favored if required power grows near the 3.5 power of length while muscle power grows near the cube, and weakened if measured flight cost scales no faster than muscle capacity.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
External morphology does not contain muscle mass or measured flight power.

Real birds change proportions with size, so a mismatch can be read as a failed prediction or as a departure from the premise.
